title: 23. Shell Expansion & Command Composition
content:
# 23. Shell Expansion & Command Composition

Shell expansion is the step where the shell turns what you typed into the arguments a command actually receives. Understanding that step prevents many quoting bugs and dangerous file operations.

## Learning goals

By the end of this module, you should be able to:

- predict how variables, globs, braces, command substitution, and word splitting behave;
- quote values correctly;
- compose commands without accidentally changing arguments;
- debug expansion by inspecting argv;
- write safer loops around filenames.

## Expansion order matters

The shell performs several expansions before running a command. The practical takeaway is simple: unquoted expansions can become multiple arguments, and globs can become filenames.

```bash
name="two words"
printf '<%s>\n' $name
printf '<%s>\n' "$name"
```

The first command receives two words. The second receives one argument.

## Variables and quoting

Default to double quotes around parameter expansions:

```bash
cp -- "$src" "$dest"
rm -- "$path"
```

Use braces when the variable name touches other characters:

```bash
printf '%s\n' "${prefix}_backup"
```

Use single quotes when you want literal text and no expansion:

```bash
printf '%s\n' '$HOME is not expanded here'
```

## Globs

Globs are expanded by the shell, not by most commands:

```bash
printf '%s\n' *.log
```

If no file matches, Bash usually leaves the pattern unchanged unless options such as `nullglob` are enabled. Scripts should not silently depend on interactive shell options.

Safer pattern:

```bash
for file in ./*.log; do
    [ -e "$file" ] || continue
    printf '%s\n' "$file"
done
```

## Brace expansion

Brace expansion creates text before variable expansion:

```bash
mkdir -p project/{src,test,docs}
printf '%s\n' file-{a,b,c}.txt
```

Because it is textual, it does not check whether files exist.

## Command substitution

Command substitution captures stdout:

```bash
current_branch=$(git branch --show-current)
```

Quote the result unless you intentionally want word splitting:

```bash
printf '%s\n' "$current_branch"
```

Command substitution strips trailing newlines, which matters when preserving exact file content.

## Arrays in Bash

Bash arrays are the right way to build argument lists dynamically:

```bash
args=(--color=auto)
[ "$verbose" = yes ] && args+=(--verbose)
grep "${args[@]}" -- "$pattern" "$file"
```

`"${args[@]}"` preserves each array element as one argument. POSIX `sh` does not have arrays.

## Pipelines and conditionals

A pipeline connects stdout from one command to stdin of the next:

```bash
journalctl -u api.service --since today | grep ERROR | tail -n 20
```

Remember that a pipeline's exit status can hide failures in earlier commands unless your shell provides and enables stricter behavior such as Bash `pipefail`.

## Inspect actual arguments

When in doubt, print arguments one per line:

```bash
printf '<%s>\n' "$@"
```

For experiments:

```bash
python3 -c 'import sys; print(sys.argv)' -- "$value"
```

## Practice

Create files with spaces, newlines, leading dashes, and glob characters in their names inside a temporary directory. Write loops that list, copy, and delete only the intended files. Verify the argv seen by each command before running destructive operations.
